title: Winding the strap (Hosea 2:21–22)
hookLine: wrapping the finger, many say "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever"

cards: A wedding ring is a small thing, a thin band of metal. Yet some people touch theirs all day without noticing, turn it when they're nervous, miss it for weeks if they take it off. It's not what it's made of.
It's what it says: I'm bound to someone, and they're bound to me. Now, the last moment of putting on tefillin. Both boxes are on.
The long strap from the arm still hangs free. The person takes it and, slowly, wraps it around one finger. Three times.

teach.b: After the head box is on, the rest of the arm strap is wound around the hand: three times around the middle finger, then across the palm, often tracing the shape of the letter shin, for Shaddai, the name from yesterday.

The customs differ: Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Hasidic Jews wind in different directions and patterns, each handed down from parents and teachers. As they wrap the finger, many say two verses from the prophet Hosea.

teach.h: I WILL BETROTH THEE UNTO ME.
teach.b: In Hosea, God speaks to the people like a spouse after a long, painful separation, promising to start again: "And I will betroth thee unto Me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto Me in righteousness, and in justice, and in lovingkindness, and in compassion. And I will betroth thee unto Me in faithfulness; and thou shalt know the LORD."
Betroth is engagement language. From the same Hebrew root comes erusin, the first stage of a Jewish marriage.
So the last act of putting on tefillin is a kind of daily wedding: the strap around the finger like a ring, and the words of a promise.

Look at what's promised: righteousness, justice, lovingkindness, compassion, faithfulness. Not a list of feelings, but of how two parties treat each other. And Hosea's words come after a story of betrayal and hurt.

teach.h: A PROMISE MADE AFTER A BREAK.
teach.b: The promise isn't made by people who've never failed each other.
It's made by people starting again. Every weekday morning, before the main prayers, the people who say these verses renew it.

how: After the head box, the arm strap is wound around the middle finger and hand; many Jews say Hosea 2:21–22 as they wrap the finger three times. Winding customs differ between Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Hasidic communities.

o: the wedding ring itself, given by the groom
betrothal, the first stage of a marriage
a promise of loyalty made between friends

games.q: you've put on both boxes. the arm strap is still hanging loose. what's the last thing you do?
o: tuck the strap into your sleeve.
wind it three times around your finger.
tie it to the head strap.
games.why: it's wound around the middle finger, like a ring, while many say Hosea's verses of betrothal.

practice: If you're wearing a ring or bracelet, touch it; if not, wrap a finger of one hand in the other.

Think of one relationship you're committed to, a partner, a friend, a parent, a child, or, if you pray, God, and choose which of Hosea's five you'd bring to it: righteousness, justice, kindness, compassion, faithfulness.
Hold the ring while you choose.

wordCard.voice: Erusin. Betrothal, the Hebrew word behind Hosea's promise, said as the tefillin strap winds three times around the finger like a ring.

orig.note: Hebrew: and I will betroth thee unto Me for ever (Hosea 2:21).

carryVoice: Your line: like a ring. A small band can carry a big promise. That's day one hundred forty-two.
